Anatomy

Anatomy · 1

Coronary arteries: origin, course and territories

How it works

The two coronary arteries leave the ascending aorta from sinuses just above the aortic valve cusps. The RCA runs in the coronary groove between right atrium and right ventricle, then posteriorly, and ends as the posterior interventricular artery. The short left main runs between the pulmonary trunk and the left auricle and divides into the circumflex and the LAD. Which artery feeds which wall follows from which groove it runs in.

What to do first

  1. Read the stenosed artery on the angiogram, then name the wall it feeds: LAD = front (sternocostal surface, anterior 2/3 of the septum, A-V bundle).
  2. Occlusion of the RCA can threaten the SA node (65%) and the AV node (80%): watch the rhythm.
  3. The septum is split: anterior 2/3 LAD, posterior 1/3 posterior interventricular artery.

Client example

A 68-year-old with recurrent angina has a 90% LAD stenosis on angiography: the anterior two thirds of the septum is at risk.

Common trap

Giving the AV node to the LAD. The LAD supplies the A-V bundle; the AV node artery comes from the RCA (80%) or circumflex (20%).

Memory trick

Anterior groove = Anterior descending = Anterior septum. RCA numbers: SA 65, AV 80.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The LAD runs in the groove with the great cardiac vein.
  • The artery to the AV node arises from the RCA in of people.

Key ideas

  • Right coronary artery: from the right (anterior) aortic sinus; left coronary artery: from the left (anterior) aortic sinus.
  • LAD runs in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the sternocostal surface of both ventricles, the anterior 2/3 of the interventricular septum and the A-V bundle.
  • The posterior interventricular artery (PDA) runs in the posterior interventricular groove and supplies the diaphragmatic surface of both ventricles and the posterior 1/3 of the septum.
  • Circumflex (LCx): branches to the left atrium and to the left ventricle, including the left (obtuse) marginal artery.
  • Artery to the SA node: RCA 65%, circumflex 35%. Artery to the AV node: RCA 80%, circumflex 20%.

Source: Anatomy L4 slides

Anatomy · 2

Coronary dominance

How it works

Dominance is named after the artery that gives the posterior interventricular artery to the diaphragmatic surface. The slide gives three patterns with their frequencies.

What to do first

  1. When a report says left dominant, expect the posterior interventricular artery from the circumflex.
  2. Note the slide's frequencies (70 / 15 / 15) and check with your instructor: many textbooks give right dominance as the most common pattern.

Client example

A client's report reads "left dominant": a circumflex occlusion could then threaten the posterior septum and diaphragmatic surface.

Common trap

Mixing co-dominance (RCA gives the PDA AND the circumflex also reaches the diaphragmatic LV) with left dominance (PDA from the circumflex).

Memory trick

Dominance = who owns the PDA.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • In left dominance the posterior interventricular artery is a branch of the artery.

Key ideas

  • Co-dominance (balanced) 70%: the right coronary has the posterior interventricular branch and the circumflex has a branch to the diaphragmatic surface of the left ventricle.
  • Right dominance (15%): the posterior interventricular artery is a large branch.
  • Left dominance (15%): the posterior interventricular artery is a large branch of the circumflex coronary.

Source: Anatomy L4 slides

Anatomy · 3

Venous drainage of the heart

How it works

Cardiac veins run with the arteries in the same grooves and drain three ways: most into the coronary sinus, which empties into the right atrium; some straight into the right atrium (anterior cardiac veins); and some straight into any chamber (venae cordis minimi).

What to do first

  1. Pair each vein with its artery: great cardiac vein with the LAD, middle cardiac vein with the posterior interventricular artery.
  2. Remember the coronary sinus ends in the posterior wall of the RIGHT atrium.

Client example

During cannulation of the coronary sinus, the nurse expects the great, middle and small cardiac veins, the posterior vein of the left ventricle and the oblique vein of the left atrium to drain through it.

Common trap

Sending the coronary sinus to the left atrium because it lies next to it. It lies between the left atrium and the diaphragmatic surface but ends in the right atrium.

Memory trick

Great goes with the Grand anterior artery (LAD); Middle goes with the middle of the back (PDA).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The anterior cardiac veins end in the .
  • Venae cordis minimi drain .

Key ideas

  • Coronary sinus: lies between the left atrium and the diaphragmatic surface and ends in the posterior wall of the right atrium.
  • Tributaries of the coronary sinus: great, middle and small cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium.
  • Anterior cardiac veins arise from the right ventricle and end in the anterior wall of the right atrium.
  • Venae cordis minimi drain directly into the cardiac chambers, especially on the right side.
  • The great cardiac vein runs with the LAD in the anterior interventricular groove; the middle cardiac vein runs with the posterior interventricular artery.

Source: Anatomy L4 slides

Anatomy · 4

Surface anatomy of the heart and valves

How it works

Four points 0.5 inch from the sternum (and the apex 3.5 inches from the midline) outline the heart on the chest wall; joining them in order gives the four borders. The valves lie in a diagonal line behind the sternum, PAMT from top left to bottom middle.

What to do first

  1. Mark A (left 2nd costal cartilage, lower border), B (right 3rd costal cartilage, upper border), C (right 6th costal cartilage), D (left 5th intercostal space).
  2. Join A-B (upper), B-C (right), C-D (lower), D-A (left).
  3. Place the valves in order: pulmonary 3rd costal cartilage, aortic 3rd space, mitral 4th cartilage, tricuspid 4th space.

Client example

Before an exam a nurse marks a client's apex at the left 5th intercostal space, 3.5 inches from the midline.

Common trap

Confusing a costal cartilage with the intercostal space below it, e.g. putting the mitral valve at the 4th space (that is the tricuspid).

Memory trick

PAMT goes down half a level at a time: P 3rd cartilage, A 3rd space, M 4th cartilage, T 4th space.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The right border of the heart runs from point to point .
  • The coronary groove is marked by a line from the left 3rd costal cartilage to point .

Key ideas

  • Point A: lower border of the left 2nd costal cartilage, 0.5 inch from the sternum; point B: upper border of the right 3rd costal cartilage, 0.5 inch from the sternum.
  • Point C: right 6th costal cartilage, 0.5 inch from the sternum; point D: left 5th intercostal space, 3.5 inches from the midline.
  • Borders: upper A-B, right B-C, lower C-D, left D-A.
  • Valves (PAMT): pulmonary behind the left 3rd costal cartilage; aortic opposite the left 3rd intercostal space; mitral opposite the left 4th costal cartilage; tricuspid opposite the left 4th intercostal space behind the midline of the sternum.

Source: Anatomy L4 slides

Anatomy · 5

Coronary angiography and PCI

How it works

Coronary angiography and PCI reach the coronary orifices from the ascending aorta by passing a catheter backwards (retrograde) up the arterial tree from the wrist or groin.

What to do first

  1. Expect local anesthesia, catheter entry through the radial or femoral artery, contrast injected into each coronary orifice, then a stent if a vessel is narrowed by plaque.

Client example

A client with a narrowed coronary artery has a stent placed after contrast pictures show the stenosis.

Common trap

Thinking the catheter is passed through a vein: it goes retrograde from the radial or femoral ARTERY.

Memory trick

In through the wrist or groin, up to the aorta, dye, picture, stent.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The catheter is passed from the radial or femoral artery into the ascending aorta.

Key ideas

  • A catheter is passed retrograde from the radial or femoral artery into the ascending aorta under local anesthesia.
  • Radiopaque contrast is injected into the orifice of each coronary artery to photograph all segments of each vessel.
  • A stent may be placed to open vessels narrowed by plaque buildup (atherosclerosis).

Source: Anatomy L4 slides

Anatomy · 6

Common, external and internal carotid arteries

How it works

The common carotid arteries start differently on each side, climb inside the carotid sheath and divide at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. The external carotid gives the face and neck their branches and ends in the parotid gland; the internal carotid gives nothing in the neck and goes straight into the skull.

What to do first

  1. Find the bifurcation at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-4).
  2. Before a jugular puncture, remember the IJV lies lateral to the artery in the sheath.
  3. Feel the superficial temporal pulse just in front of the tragus.

Client example

An anesthesiologist at the head of the table checks the pulse in front of the tragus: the superficial temporal artery.

Common trap

Looking for neck branches on the internal carotid. It has none; all named neck branches are from the external carotid or subclavian.

Memory trick

ECA branches in order: Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students (superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, maxillary, superficial temporal).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The external carotid ends in the behind the neck of the mandible.
  • The right common carotid arises from the .

Key ideas

  • Right common carotid: from the brachiocephalic artery behind the sternoclavicular joint; left common carotid: from the arch of the aorta.
  • The common carotid ascends in the carotid sheath, related medially to the trachea and larynx and laterally to the IJV, and ends at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3-4).
  • The external carotid ends in the parotid gland behind the neck of the mandible by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.
  • External carotid branches: superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, superficial temporal and maxillary.
  • The internal carotid has no branches in the neck; it enters the skull through the carotid canal.

Source: Anatomy L5 slides

Anatomy · 7

Subclavian artery

How it works

Scalenus anterior crosses in front of the subclavian artery and so divides it into three parts. Each part has its own branches, and the artery ends at the outer border of the 1st rib by becoming the axillary artery.

What to do first

  1. Sort branches by part: 1st = vertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical trunk; 2nd = costocervical trunk; 3rd = dorsal scapular.
  2. Remember the thyrocervical trunk gives the inferior thyroid, transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries.

Client example

During thyroid surgery near the thyrocervical trunk, the inferior thyroid artery is at risk, not the superior thyroid (an external carotid branch).

Common trap

Mixing the superior thyroid artery (external carotid) with the inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk).

Memory trick

1st part 3 branches, 2nd part 1 trunk, 3rd part 1 branch.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the outer border of the .
  • The costocervical trunk arises from the part of the subclavian artery.

Key ideas

  • Right subclavian: from the brachiocephalic artery behind the right sternoclavicular joint; left subclavian: from the arch of the aorta.
  • It ends at the outer border of the 1st rib by becoming the axillary artery.
  • Scalenus anterior passes anterior to the artery and divides it into 3 parts: medial, behind and lateral to the muscle.
  • 1st part: vertebral, internal thoracic and thyrocervical trunk (inferior thyroid, transverse cervical, suprascapular). 2nd part: costocervical trunk. 3rd part: dorsal scapular (66%).

Source: Anatomy L5 slides

Anatomy · 8

Facial veins and the dangerous area of the face

How it works

The facial veins join and divide around the parotid gland. The anterior facial vein links to the cavernous sinus inside the skull through the ophthalmic veins and through the deep facial vein and pterygoid plexus, which is why the nose and upper lip are the dangerous area.

What to do first

  1. Teach clients not to squeeze lesions on the nose and upper lip: infection can reach the cavernous sinus.
  2. Trace formation: supraorbital + supratrochlear = anterior facial; maxillary + superficial temporal = retromandibular; anterior facial + anterior division of retromandibular = common facial (to IJV).

Client example

A client squeezes an infected pimple on the upper lip; the nurse is concerned about spread to the cavernous sinus.

Common trap

Thinking the route goes through the jugular veins. The dangerous route runs backwards from the anterior facial vein into the skull.

Memory trick

Dangerous triangle: nose and upper lip drain back to the brain.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The deep facial vein connects the anterior facial vein to the .
  • The retromandibular vein is formed inside the .

Key ideas

  • Anterior facial vein: formed by the supraorbital and supratrochlear veins at the medial angle of the eye.
  • Retromandibular (posterior facial) vein: formed by the maxillary and superficial temporal veins inside the parotid gland; divides at the lower pole of the parotid.
  • Common facial vein: anterior facial vein + anterior division of the retromandibular vein; drains into the IJV.
  • The deep facial vein connects the anterior facial vein to the pterygoid plexus.
  • Dangerous area of the face (nose and upper lip): infection can reach the cavernous sinus through the connections of the anterior facial vein.

Source: Anatomy L5 slides

Anatomy · 9

Jugular, subclavian and brachiocephalic veins

How it works

Blood from the head reaches the heart by two jugular veins. The external jugular is superficial and drains into the subclavian vein; the internal jugular is deep, begins at the jugular foramen and joins the subclavian to form the brachiocephalic vein. Both brachiocephalic veins form the SVC.

What to do first

  1. Sort tributaries: EJV = transverse cervical, suprascapular, anterior jugular; IJV = pharyngeal, common facial, lingual, superior and middle thyroid.
  2. Trace face to heart: anterior facial, common facial, IJV, brachiocephalic, SVC.

Client example

A nurse sees a distended vein crossing sternomastoid: the external jugular vein, formed by the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein.

Common trap

Draining the external jugular into the internal jugular. It ends in the subclavian vein.

Memory trick

External ends External-ish (subclavian); Internal starts Inside the skull (sigmoid sinus).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The internal jugular vein begins as the continuation of the .
  • The external jugular vein ends in the .

Key ideas

  • External jugular vein: formed by the posterior division of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein; descends superficial to sternomastoid; ends in the subclavian vein.
  • External jugular tributaries: transverse cervical, suprascapular and anterior jugular veins.
  • Internal jugular vein: begins as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus at the jugular foramen; joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
  • Internal jugular tributaries: pharyngeal, common facial, lingual, superior thyroid and middle thyroid veins.
  • Right and left brachiocephalic veins unite to form the SVC.

Source: Anatomy L5 slides

Physiology

Physiology · 1

ECG leads and what they record

How it works

The heart's electrical activity creates potential differences that the body, a good conductor, carries to the skin. Each lead is a picture of that activity from one direction: limb leads in the frontal plane, chest leads in the horizontal plane. Einthoven's triangle is formed by the axes of the limb leads around the heart.

What to do first

  1. Check electrode placement before recording: wrong leads give wrong pictures.
  2. Read a deflection by direction: toward the electrode = up, away = down.
  3. Localize changes by lead group: inferior II, III, aVF; lateral I, aVL, V5, V6; septal V1, V2; anterior V3, V4.

Client example

A nurse reassures an anxious client that the ECG only records electrical activity; it does not measure blood flow.

Common trap

Thinking the ECG measures how well blood is pumped. It records electrical events only.

Memory trick

Bipolar = the Big three (I, II, III); augmented = the aV letters.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • In a bipolar lead the potential difference is recorded between .
  • Leads II, III and aVF view the portion of the heart.

Key ideas

  • The ECG measures the electrical activity of the heart per unit time; it does NOT measure the flow of blood through the heart.
  • Six limb leads (frontal plane): bipolar I, II, III and unipolar augmented aVR, aVL, aVF. Six precordial leads V1-V6 (horizontal plane).
  • Current flowing towards the recording electrode gives an upward deflection; current flowing away gives a downward deflection.
  • Views: left lateral I, aVL, V5, V6; septum V1, V2; anterior V3, V4; inferior II, III, aVF.

Source: Physiology L6 slides (ECG I)

Physiology · 2

ECG paper, waves and intervals

How it works

Paper speed converts time to distance: at 25 mm/s each 1 mm is 0.04 s. Each wave marks a step in the conduction sequence SA node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibers.

What to do first

  1. Measure intervals horizontally: small box 0.04 s, large box 0.20 s.
  2. Check PR 0.12-0.20 s, QRS 0.08-0.10 s, QT 0.40-0.43 s.
  3. Remember the PR includes the AV-junction delay that lets the atria finish contracting.

Client example

A nurse counts 5 small boxes for a PR interval: 5 x 0.04 = 0.20 s, the upper limit of normal.

Common trap

Reading the vertical 0.5 mV as a time, or using 0.20 s for a small box.

Memory trick

P = atria, QRS = ventricles go, T = ventricles recover.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The T wave represents ventricular .
  • One large box horizontally equals s.

Key ideas

  • Paper speed is 25 mm/sec: one small box = 0.04 s, one large box = 0.20 s; vertically one large box = 0.5 mV.
  • P wave = atrial depolarization; QRS = ventricular depolarization; T wave = ventricular repolarization.
  • PR interval = atrial depolarization + delay in the AV junction; the delay lets the atria contract before the ventricles.
  • PR 0.12-0.20 s; QRS 0.08-0.10 s; QT 0.40-0.43 s.

Source: Physiology L6 slides (ECG I)

Physiology · 3

Rhythm analysis and heart rate

How it works

Because paper runs at a fixed speed, the R-R distance gives the rate: there are 1500 small squares or 300 large squares in a minute. Dividing by the squares between beats gives beats per minute.

What to do first

  1. Analyze in order: regularity, rate, P waves, PR interval, QRS duration.
  2. Use 1500 with small squares and 300 with large squares.
  3. Quick count from an R on a heavy line: 300, 150, 100, 75.

Client example

R-R = 20 small squares: 1500 / 20 = 75 beats/min.

Common trap

Dividing 300 by small squares (or 1500 by large squares).

Memory trick

Small with big number (1500), big with small number (300).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • HR = divided by the number of small squares between R waves.
  • If the next R wave is 3 large boxes away, the rate is .

Key ideas

  • Steps: 1 regularity, 2 rate, 3 P waves, 4 PR interval, 5 QRS duration.
  • HR = 1500 / number of small squares between R-R, or 300 / number of large squares.
  • Large boxes to the next R wave: 1 = 300, 2 = 150, 3 = 100, 4 = 75.

Source: Physiology L7 slides (ECG II)

Physiology · 4

Normal sinus rhythm and its variations

How it works

A sinus rhythm starts in the SA node and conducts normally, so every P is normal and followed by a QRS. Only the rate (or its variation with breathing) changes in the sinus variants.

What to do first

  1. If P, PR and QRS are normal, name the rhythm by rate: slow = sinus bradycardia, fast = sinus tachycardia.
  2. If the rate rises with inspiration and falls with expiration, call it sinus arrhythmia.

Client example

Rate 35, regular, normal P, PR 0.12 s, QRS 0.10 s: sinus bradycardia.

Common trap

Calling every slow rhythm a heart block. Check whether every P is followed by a QRS.

Memory trick

Sinus arrhythmia breathes with the client: in = faster.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • In sinus arrhythmia the heart rate during inspiration.

Key ideas

  • Normal sinus rhythm: regular, normal P waves with one P for every QRS, PR 0.12-0.20 s, normal QRS.
  • Sinus bradycardia: everything normal but a slow rate (35 bpm on the slide); sinus tachycardia: normal but fast (130 bpm).
  • Sinus arrhythmia: heart rate increases during inspiration and decreases during expiration.

Source: Physiology L7 slides (ECG II)

Physiology · 5

Atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter

How it works

In atrial fibrillation the atria have no organized depolarization because impulses are not coming from the sinus node, so there are no P waves and the ventricles respond irregularly. In atrial flutter, flutter waves replace the P waves.

What to do first

  1. Look for P waves first: none and irregularly irregular = atrial fibrillation.
  2. Flutter waves with a regular rhythm = atrial flutter.

Client example

An 84-year-old client's strip shows no P waves and an irregularly irregular rate: atrial fibrillation.

Common trap

Confusing the regularly irregular pattern of Mobitz I with the irregularly irregular pattern of AF.

Memory trick

AF: Absent P, Frenzied atria (over 350).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • In atrial fibrillation the atrial rate is usually above per minute.

Key ideas

  • Atrial fibrillation: no organized atrial depolarization, so no normal P waves; atrial rate usually above 350/min; irregularly irregular.
  • Atrial fibrillation affects 2-4%, up to 5-10% of people over 80 years old.
  • Atrial flutter: flutter waves instead of P waves, no measurable PR interval; rhythm regular in the slide example.

Source: Physiology L7 slides (ECG II)

Physiology · 6

AV nodal blocks

How it works

AV blocks grade how much gets through the AV junction: all but slowly (1st degree), progressively slower until one fails (Mobitz I), all or nothing (Mobitz II, usually in the bundle of His), or nothing at all (3rd degree). When the ventricles must pace themselves, the impulse starts in a ventricle and the QRS is wide.

What to do first

  1. Measure the PR on every beat: constant and long = 1st degree; lengthening then dropped = Mobitz I; constant with sudden drops = Mobitz II.
  2. If P waves have no relation to QRS and the rate is 30-45 with wide QRS, think 3rd degree.

Client example

PR 0.36 s, every P conducted, regular rate 60: first-degree AV block.

Common trap

Mixing Mobitz I (PR lengthens) with Mobitz II (PR constant).

Memory trick

Mobitz I: longer, longer, longer, drop. Mobitz II: steady, steady, drop.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • In 3rd-degree block the ventricular pacemaker fires at about beats/minute.
  • Mobitz type II block is typically located in the .

Key ideas

  • 1st degree: PR interval > 0.20 s; prolonged conduction delay in the AV node or bundle of His.
  • 2nd degree Mobitz I: PR progressively lengthens until one impulse (usually the 3rd or 4th) fails to make it through the AV node.
  • 2nd degree Mobitz II: occasional P waves are completely blocked with no PR prolongation (all or nothing); block typically in the bundle of His.
  • 3rd degree: complete block in the AV junction; atria and ventricles beat independently; ventricular pacemaker at 30-45 beats/minute.
  • When an impulse originates in a ventricle, conduction is inefficient and the QRS is wide and bizarre.

Source: Physiology L7 slides (ECG II)

Physiology · 7

Mean QRS axis

How it works

The mean QRS axis is the sum of all ventricular depolarization vectors. Normally it points left and down because the left ventricle has most of the mass. On the hexaxial circle, 0 degrees points to the client's left and degrees increase clockwise, so +90 points down.

What to do first

  1. Check lead I and aVF: + + normal; + - left; - + right; - - right superior (indeterminate).
  2. Report an abnormal axis: it can suggest disease such as pulmonary hypertension from pulmonary embolism.

Client example

Lead I positive, aVF negative: left axis deviation.

Common trap

Reversing left and right: a NEGATIVE lead I means the vector points to the right.

Memory trick

Two thumbs up (I and aVF positive) = normal.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The normal QRS axis lies between and degrees.

Key ideas

  • Normal ventricular depolarization flows leftward and downward because most of the ventricular mass is in the left ventricle.
  • Normal QRS axis: -30 to +110 degrees. Left axis deviation: -30 to -90. Right axis deviation: +110 to +180. Indeterminate (extreme right): +180 to -90.
  • Lead I and aVF: + + normal; + - left axis deviation; - + right axis deviation; - - right superior / indeterminate.
  • An abnormal axis can suggest disease such as pulmonary hypertension from a pulmonary embolism.

Source: Physiology L7 slides (ECG II)

Physiology · 8

Cardiac output, stroke volume and ejection fraction

How it works

Cardiac output is how much each ventricle pumps per minute: rate times stroke volume. Stroke volume is the difference between how full the ventricle gets (EDV) and how much is left (ESV); ejection fraction expresses it as a percentage of EDV and is a good index of ventricular function.

What to do first

  1. Calculate CO = HR x SV and convert mL to L.
  2. Calculate SV = EDV - ESV, then EF = SV / EDV x 100.
  3. Flag an EF of 30% or less as consistent with a failing heart.

Client example

EDV 125 mL, ESV 50 mL: SV 75 mL, EF 75/125 x 100 = 60%.

Common trap

Putting ESV instead of SV on top of the EF fraction.

Memory trick

EF = what left / what was there.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Normal ejection fraction is about .
  • Normal cardiac index is L/min/m2.

Key ideas

  • Cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume = 70 x 70 = 4900 ml/min, about 5 L/min.
  • Stroke volume = EDV - ESV (about 70-80 ml); EDV about 120-130 ml; ESV about 50-60 ml.
  • EF = SV / EDV x 100; normal 50-75%, up to 90% in strenuous exercise; 30% or less in a failing heart.
  • Cardiac index = cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface area; normal 3.2 L/min/m2.
  • Cardiac reserve = the difference between cardiac output at rest and the maximum the heart can pump per minute.

Source: Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output)

Physiology · 9

Autonomic control of heart rate and contractility

How it works

The vagus reaches mainly the atria (SA and AV nodes), so it can slow the rate and AV conduction but cannot touch ventricular contractility. Sympathetic fibers reach the nodes AND the ventricles, so they speed the rate and conduction and strengthen both atria and ventricles; they also release adrenal epinephrine.

What to do first

  1. Predict vagal effects: slower rate, longer AV delay, weaker atria, ventricles unchanged.
  2. Predict sympathetic effects: faster rate, shorter AV delay, stronger atria and ventricles.

Client example

A frightened client's sympathetic surge raises the heart rate and ventricular contractility.

Common trap

Giving the vagus an effect on ventricular muscle: it has none.

Memory trick

Vagus = brakes on the top floor only (atria).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Parasympathetic stimulation AV nodal delay.
  • At rest, discharge dominates heart rate.

Key ideas

  • Parasympathetic (vagus) mainly supplies the atria (SA and AV nodes); parasympathetic innervation of the ventricles is sparse.
  • Parasympathetic: decreases heart rate, increases AV nodal delay, decreases atrial contractility, no effect on ventricular muscle.
  • Sympathetic: increases heart rate, decreases AV nodal delay, hastens ventricular conduction, increases atrial and ventricular contractility, promotes adrenal epinephrine.
  • Under resting conditions parasympathetic discharge dominates.

Source: Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output)

Physiology · 10

Frank-Starling law, preload and afterload

How it works

Cardiac fibers at rest are shorter than their optimum length. More filling stretches them toward optimum, so the next contraction is stronger: the Frank-Starling law (intrinsic control). Sympathetic stimulation is extrinsic: it raises contractility at any filling by increasing Ca2+ influx, shifting the curve to the left.

What to do first

  1. Link a rise in EDV (preload) to a stronger contraction through Frank-Starling.
  2. Link sympathetic stimulation to a left shift of the curve.
  3. Keep the loads apart: preload = EDV; afterload = arterial pressure.

Client example

A fluid bolus raises EDV and the stroke volume rises: Frank-Starling.

Common trap

Calling EDV afterload.

Memory trick

PRE comes before contraction (filling); AFTER is what the ventricle pushes against.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The extent of filling is referred to as .
  • Sympathetic stimulation shifts the Frank-Starling curve to the .

Key ideas

  • Frank-Starling law: force of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fiber (EDV and stroke volume).
  • Resting cardiac fiber length is less than optimum, so more filling stretches fibers closer to optimum and increases the force of the next contraction.
  • Preload = load before contraction, the end-diastolic volume. Afterload = load the ventricle pumps against, the arterial blood pressure.
  • Sympathetic stimulation and epinephrine increase contractility at any EDV (more Ca2+ influx) and shift the Frank-Starling curve to the left.

Source: Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output)

Physiology · 11

Factors controlling venous return

How it works

Veins are capacitance vessels holding 60-70% of the blood. Anything that squeezes them or pulls blood toward the chest moves blood back to the heart and raises EDV.

What to do first

  1. Encourage leg exercise (muscle pump) and deep breathing (respiratory pump) in clients on bed rest.
  2. Remember sympathetic venoconstriction, cardiac suction and venous valves also help.

Client example

A client on bed rest does leg exercises; muscle contraction compresses the veins and increases venous return.

Common trap

Thinking veins storing more blood increases return. Less storage means more return.

Memory trick

Squeeze, suck, shut: muscle pump squeezes, inspiration and cardiac suction suck, valves shut backflow.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • During inspiration, intrathoracic pressure falls to about mmHg.
  • Venous valves are placed at cm intervals.

Key ideas

  • Veins are capacitance vessels holding about 60-70% of blood; when veins store less blood, more returns to the heart.
  • Skeletal muscle pump: contraction compresses veins and moves blood toward the heart.
  • Respiratory pump: in inspiration intrathoracic pressure falls (-5 mmHg), drawing blood into the chest.
  • Sympathetic venoconstriction, the cardiac suction effect and one-way venous valves (every 2-4 cm) also increase venous return.

Source: Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output)

Physiology · 12

Measuring cardiac output and conditions that change it

How it works

The Fick principle says the oxygen the lungs take up equals blood flow times the oxygen each liter picks up. So flow (cardiac output) = O2 uptake / arterial-venous O2 difference, with venous blood taken from the pulmonary artery.

What to do first

  1. Set up Fick: O2 uptake (mL/min) / (arterial - venous O2, mL/L).
  2. Recognize conditions that raise CO (hyperthyroidism, anemia, fever) and lower it (hypothyroidism, failure, valve disease, arrhythmias, hemorrhage).

Client example

O2 uptake 250 mL/min, A-V difference 50 mL/L: cardiac output 5 L/min.

Common trap

Dividing by arterial O2 content instead of the A-V difference.

Memory trick

Fick: flow = uptake / difference.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Cardiac output can also be measured by dye dilution and combined with echocardiography.

Key ideas

  • Fick principle: cardiac output = O2 uptake by the lungs / (arterial O2 - venous O2), e.g. 200 / (200 - 160) = 5 L/min.
  • Cardiac output rises in hyperthyroidism, anemia and fever; falls in hypothyroidism, myocardial damage and failure, valvular disease, arrhythmias, hemorrhage and shock.
  • Most common causes of heart failure: myocardial infarction, then working against increased afterload (hypertension, aortic stenosis).

Source: Physiology L8 slides (cardiac output)

Physiology · 13

Coronary blood flow and oxygen extraction

How it works

Cardiac muscle is packed with mitochondria and works aerobically, so it already takes 60-70% of the oxygen it receives. With so little left to extract, more oxygen can reach it only by more flow.

What to do first

  1. Expect symptoms when demand rises and flow cannot: angina on effort.
  2. Link ischemic pain to lactic acid from anaerobic glycolysis.

Client example

A client with coronary disease starts exercising; the heart can meet the extra demand only by increasing coronary flow.

Common trap

Thinking the heart can extract much more oxygen when needed, like other tissues.

Memory trick

Heart takes two thirds already; it needs more flow, not more extraction.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • At rest the heart extracts of oxygen; other tissues extract about .

Key ideas

  • Coronary blood flow at rest is about 225-250 ml/minute, about 5% of cardiac output.
  • At rest the heart extracts 60-70% of the oxygen from each unit of blood (other tissues about 25%).
  • Up to 40% of the cardiac cell is mitochondria, so the heart needs more O2; when more O2 is needed, delivery rises only by increasing blood flow.
  • The heart uses mainly free fatty acids; in ischemia it uses anaerobic glycolysis, forming lactic acid (one cause of cardiac pain).

Source: Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation)

Physiology · 14

Phasic changes in coronary flow

How it works

The left ventricle squeezes its own coronary vessels in systole and the open aortic valve partly covers their openings, so left ventricular flow happens mainly in diastole. The right ventricle's lower pressure leaves a large aorta-RV gradient in systole, so its flow is preserved.

What to do first

  1. Treat tachycardia as a threat to coronary flow because diastole shortens.
  2. Expect the LV subendocardium to be hit first in ischemia.
  3. Remember aortic stenosis and low aortic diastolic pressure reduce LV flow.

Client example

A client with a rate of 150 complains of chest tightness: shortened diastole reduces coronary flow.

Common trap

Thinking a faster rate improves coronary flow.

Memory trick

The left heart feeds itself between beats.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • In systole the aorta-to-left-ventricle pressure gradient is about mmHg.
  • The most common site of myocardial infarction is the layer of the left ventricle.

Key ideas

  • Left ventricular flow falls in systole: the contracting LV compresses the coronary arteries and the open aortic valve partially blocks their entrance.
  • Systole: aorta 120, LV 121 mmHg (gradient -1); diastole: aorta 80, LV 0 (gradient 80). Right ventricle gradient is 95 in systole, 80 in diastole.
  • The subendocardial surface of the left ventricle gets almost no flow in systole, so it is the most common site of myocardial infarction.
  • Tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces coronary flow; aortic stenosis and low aortic diastolic pressure also reduce LV flow.

Source: Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation)

Physiology · 15

Chemical and neural control of coronary flow

How it works

Coronary flow follows metabolism: working muscle produces CO2, H+, K+, lactate, adenosine and other metabolites, and lack of oxygen itself dilates the vessels. Sympathetic nerves act two ways: directly they constrict (alpha), but indirectly, by making the heart work harder (beta-1), they release dilating metabolites, which wins in the intact body.

What to do first

  1. Expect coronary dilation in hypoxia and with local metabolites (adenosine).
  2. Explain that beta blockade unmasks the direct constrictor effect of norepinephrine.

Client example

In shock, reflex sympathetic discharge raises coronary flow through metabolic changes while other organs are compromised.

Common trap

Assuming the direct sympathetic effect on coronaries is dilation.

Memory trick

Directly: Constrict. Indirectly: Increase work, Increase flow.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Adenosine is formed from during cardiac metabolic activity.
  • Parasympathetic influences on coronary vessels are minor and weakly .

Key ideas

  • Coronary blood flow shows considerable autoregulation.
  • Vasodilators: lack of oxygen, increased CO2, H+, K+, lactate, prostaglandins, adenosine and adenine nucleotides.
  • Adenosine, formed from ATP during cardiac metabolic activity, causes coronary vasodilatation.
  • Direct sympathetic effect: alpha-receptor vasoconstriction (seen when beta receptors are blocked). Indirect effect in the intact body: beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility, releasing vasodilator metabolites.
  • Parasympathetic influences are minor and weakly vasodilatory.

Source: Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation)

Physiology · 16

Ischemic heart disease and myocardial infarction

How it works

Atherosclerotic plaque narrows the coronary lumen. When demand rises, flow cannot keep up and the client gets angina; when a thrombus blocks at least 75% of the lumen, myocardium dies (MI). The ECG separates them: ST depression in ischemia, ST elevation in infarction.

What to do first

  1. Ask about effort-related retrosternal pain relieved by rest.
  2. Report ST elevation in a client with chest pain as consistent with MI.
  3. Expect investigations: ECG, cardiac enzymes (CK, LDH, troponin), echo, treadmill, thallium, angiography.

Client example

An exercise test shows horizontal ST depression: ischemic heart disease.

Common trap

Mixing up ST depression (angina) and ST elevation (MI).

Memory trick

Elevation = Emergency (infarct); Depression = Demand ischemia.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Treatment of IHD includes coronary dilators such as , beta-blockers, angioplasty, stents and bypass surgery.

Key ideas

  • Risk factors of IHD: cigarette smoking, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, increased lipids (cholesterol), lack of exercise, anxiety.
  • Angina: retrosternal tightness or pain for a few minutes, often radiating to the inner side of the left arm, precipitated by effort and relieved by rest.
  • MI: at least 75% of the coronary lumen blocked by thrombus.
  • ECG: ST depression in IHD; ST elevation in MI, in the respective leads.
  • Treatment: coronary dilators (nitrates), beta-blockers, angioplasty, stent, bypass surgery.

Source: Physiology L9 slides (coronary circulation)

Pathology

Pathology · 1

Hyperemia and congestion

How it works

Both hyperemia and congestion mean more blood in a tissue, with dilated capillaries and a risk of edema. The difference is the direction of the problem: hyperemia is active arterial inflow (red, oxygenated), congestion is passive venous outflow failure (blue, deoxygenated). Chronic left failure or mitral stenosis congests the lungs, producing heart failure cells and brown induration.

What to do first

  1. Use color to tell them apart: red = hyperemia, dusky blue = congestion.
  2. Link chronic right-sided failure to generalized congestion and cardiac edema.
  3. Link chronic left-sided failure and mitral stenosis to pulmonary congestion.

Client example

A client with a DVT has a dusky reddish-blue swollen leg: acute localized congestion.

Common trap

Calling the red face of exercise or blushing congestion; it is hyperemia.

Memory trick

Hyperemia is Hot and red (active); congestion is Clogged and blue (passive).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages are called .
  • Long-standing pulmonary congestion with fibrosis causes of the lung.

Key ideas

  • Hyperemia: an active process in which arteriolar dilation increases blood flow; tissue turns red (erythema) from oxygenated blood.
  • Congestion: a passive process from impaired venous outflow; tissue is dusky reddish-blue (cyanosis) from deoxygenated blood.
  • Acute localized congestion: sudden complete venous obstruction (DVT, ligature, twisted pedicle of an ovary) causing rapid edema and hemorrhage.
  • Chronic generalized venous congestion is caused by chronic right-sided heart failure; acute generalized congestion by acute heart failure.

Source: Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I)

Pathology · 2

Edema: causes and classification

How it works

Fluid leaves capillaries when the pushing force rises (hydrostatic pressure), the holding force falls (colloid osmotic pressure), the wall leaks (permeability) or the drain is blocked (lymphatics). Edema fluid may be a transudate, an exudate or lymph.

What to do first

  1. Match the cause to the mechanism before choosing a treatment focus.
  2. Press the skin: pitting suggests generalized or venous edema; non-pitting suggests inflammatory or lymphatic edema.

Client example

A malnourished client with serum albumin below 1.5 gm% develops nutritional edema from low colloid osmotic pressure.

Common trap

Expecting lymphatic edema (e.g. filariasis) to pit.

Memory trick

Four ways to flood: push up, pull down, leak, block.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Fluid in the pleural cavity is called .
  • Generalized edema due to renal failure is called edema.

Key ideas

  • Edema: an abnormal increase in interstitial fluid within tissues; fluid may be transudate, exudate or lymph.
  • Causes: increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure, increased capillary permeability, lymphatic obstruction.
  • Hypoproteinemia: total plasma proteins below 2.5 gm% or serum albumin below 1.5 gm%.
  • Pitting edema: generalized edema and obstructive venous edema. Non-pitting: inflammatory and lymphatic edema.

Source: Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I)

Pathology · 3

Ischemia and infarction

How it works

Ischemia is too little arterial supply. Whether it kills tissue depends on speed and collaterals: sudden complete occlusion in an organ with poor collaterals gives an infarct. Infarct color depends on whether blood can seep in: loose tissue, dual supply, venous occlusion or reperfusion give red infarcts; dense end-arterial organs give white ones.

What to do first

  1. Predict red vs white from the organ: lung, liver, intestine, ovary red; heart, spleen, kidney white.
  2. Think venous infarction in organs with a single venous outflow (testis, ovary).

Client example

After angioplasty restores flow to an infarcted area, the infarct turns red (reperfusion).

Common trap

Calling a lung infarct white.

Memory trick

Solid organs, end arteries, white (heart, spleen, kidney).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • About of infarcts result from thrombosis or embolism.
  • Infarcts are also classified as septic or (aseptic).

Key ideas

  • Ischemia: deficient arterial blood supply due to partial or complete occlusion of the artery; acute (sudden complete) or chronic (gradual partial).
  • Organs with good collateral circulation show no effect; poor collateral circulation leads to infarction (acute) or chronic ischemic changes.
  • Infarct: an area of ischemic necrosis from occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage; 99% from thrombosis or embolism.
  • Red infarct: venous occlusion (ovary), loose tissue (lung), dual circulation (lung, liver, small intestine), reperfusion after angioplasty.
  • White infarct: arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (heart, spleen, kidney); tissue density limits seepage of blood.

Source: Pathology L1 slides (hemodynamic disorders I)

Pathology · 4

Thrombosis and Virchow's triad

How it works

Hemostasis depends on the vessel wall, platelets and coagulation factors. Virchow's triad names the three ways it tips into thrombosis: damaged or dysfunctional endothelium, abnormal flow (stasis or turbulence), and blood that clots too easily.

What to do first

  1. Screen surgical and immobile clients for all three triad factors.
  2. Separate hereditary (factor V, prothrombin gene, antithrombin III deficiency) from acquired hypercoagulability.

Client example

A postoperative client on bed rest has stasis and acquired hypercoagulability: two arms of the triad.

Common trap

Listing edema mechanisms (permeability, lymphatic obstruction) as causes of thrombosis.

Memory trick

Virchow = Vessel wall, Velocity (flow), Viscosity-like clotting (hypercoagulability).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Turbulence endothelial cells.
  • DIC is an cause of hypercoagulability.

Key ideas

  • Thrombosis: formation of a compact mass of circulating blood elements inside the cardiovascular system during life.
  • Virchow's triad: endothelial injury/dysfunction, alterations in blood flow (stasis or turbulence), hypercoagulability.
  • Endothelial dysfunction increases procoagulants (thromboplastin, vWF, PAI) and decreases anticoagulants (thrombomodulin, antithrombin III, NO, PA).
  • Stasis reduces inflow of fresh blood containing natural anticoagulants and retards removal of small platelet aggregates.
  • Acquired hypercoagulability: prolonged bed rest, surgery, burns, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, disseminated cancer, smoking, DIC. Hereditary: factor V and prothrombin gene mutations, antithrombin III deficiency.

Source: Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II)

Pathology · 5

Sites, types and fate of thrombi

How it works

Where a thrombus forms depends on local conditions: slow venous flow plus hypercoagulability gives venous (red) thrombi; atherosclerotic arteries give arterial thrombi; stasis in a dilated atrium or over an infarct gives cardiac thrombi. Once formed, a thrombus can dissolve, grow, break off or be organized.

What to do first

  1. Monitor a client with DVT for pulmonary embolism.
  2. Watch for propagation: a tail makes detachment more likely.

Client example

A client with mitral stenosis develops an auricular thrombus in the left atrium.

Common trap

Thinking arterial thrombi are most common. Venous thrombi are.

Memory trick

Veins: slow and sticky; arteries: fast and thick-walled.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Thrombi of infected veins are called .
  • Septic thrombi that embolize produce .

Key ideas

  • Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis, red thrombi) are the most common type, associated with stasis and hypercoagulability.
  • DVT sites: popliteal, femoral and iliac veins; complication: embolism to the lungs (pulmonary infarction).
  • Arterial thrombosis is less common because of rapid flow and the thick elastic arterial wall; most common cause is atherosclerosis (coronary, cerebral, femoral).
  • Cardiac thrombi: auricular thrombus in the left atrium in mitral stenosis; mural thrombus in the left ventricle over an infarct; vegetations on valves.
  • Fate: dissolution, propagation (a tail liable to detach), embolization, organization and recanalization.

Source: Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II)

Pathology · 6

Embolism and pulmonary embolism

How it works

An embolus is anything solid, liquid or gas carried away from where it formed. Almost all are thromboemboli, and almost all pulmonary emboli come from leg DVT. What happens next depends on embolus size and the state of the lung.

What to do first

  1. Suspect PE in a postoperative or immobile client with sudden dyspnea.
  2. Expect a saddle embolus to cause sudden death from acute right-sided failure.

Client example

A client with heart failure and lung congestion gets a medium embolus: pulmonary infarction.

Common trap

Expecting a medium embolus in a healthy lung to infarct; it causes hemorrhage only.

Memory trick

Big = dead, medium = depends on the lung, small and many = pulmonary hypertension.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • About of pulmonary emboli are small and clinically silent.

Key ideas

  • An embolus is a detached intravascular solid, liquid or gaseous mass carried by the blood to a site distant from its origin.
  • Thromboemboli are the most common type (99%); others: fat, parasitic, air or nitrogen, amniotic fluid, tumor, cholesterol and foreign body emboli.
  • Pulmonary emboli: 95% originate from deep vein thrombi of the legs; seen in up to 25-30% of DVT patients; 60-80% are small and silent.
  • Saddle embolus causes sudden death (acute right failure); medium emboli give hemorrhage in a normal lung or infarction in a congested lung; small repeated emboli give pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.

Source: Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II)

Pathology · 7

Systemic, fat, air and amniotic fluid emboli

How it works

Systemic emboli travel in arteries, so they come from the left heart or arteries. A venous embolus reaches the systemic side only through a septal defect (paradoxical). Fat, air and amniotic fluid emboli each have a typical setting.

What to do first

  1. After a large MI, check limb pulses: most systemic emboli lodge in the legs.
  2. Two days after a long bone fracture, watch for fat embolism syndrome.
  3. During delivery, sudden dyspnea, shock, seizures and bleeding suggest amniotic fluid embolism.

Client example

A client with an atrial septal defect and DVT has a stroke: paradoxical embolism.

Common trap

Sending a leg DVT embolus to the brain without a septal defect.

Memory trick

Fat after fracture, air after access, amniotic at delivery.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Fat embolism syndrome is fatal in about of cases.
  • Decompression sickness is also called disease.

Key ideas

  • Systemic emboli: 80% from intracardiac thrombi (2/3 left ventricular wall infarcts, 1/3 dilated left atria or vegetations); also aortic aneurysm, ulcerated plaques, paradoxical emboli.
  • Paradoxical emboli start as venous emboli but pass through an interatrial or interventricular defect into the systemic circulation.
  • Site of arrest: 75% lower extremities, 10% brain.
  • Fat embolism: long bone fracture is the most common cause; the syndrome begins 1-3 days after injury with tachypnea, dyspnea, tachycardia, neurologic symptoms, thrombocytopenia and anemia.
  • Air embolism needs more than 100 cc of air for a pulmonary effect; causes include neck vein injury, chest wall injury, obstetric or laparoscopic procedures, bypass surgery and decompression sickness.
  • Amniotic fluid embolism: 1 in 40,000 deliveries, mortality 80%; sudden dyspnea, cyanosis, shock, seizures, pulmonary edema and DIC.

Source: Pathology L2 slides (hemodynamic disorders II)

Pathology · 8

Acute rheumatic fever: pathogenesis and lesions

How it works

Weeks after strep throat, antibodies and T cells made against streptococcal M proteins cross-react with heart antigens. Complement and macrophages are activated and Aschoff bodies form in every layer of the heart, giving pancarditis.

What to do first

  1. Ask about a sore throat 10 days to 6 weeks before.
  2. Recognize Aschoff bodies and Anitschkow cells as pathognomonic.
  3. Prompt antibiotic treatment of strep pharyngitis prevents disease.

Client example

A 14-year-old with a sore throat 3 weeks ago, fever, nodules and a new apical murmur: biopsy shows fibrinoid necrosis with histiocytes.

Common trap

Thinking the streptococcus infects the heart directly; the damage is immune cross-reaction.

Memory trick

M protein Mimics heart.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Anitschkow cells are also called cells.
  • Rheumatic vegetations overlie foci of .

Key ideas

  • ARF is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease a few weeks after group A streptococcal pharyngitis.
  • It appears 10 days to 6 weeks after pharyngitis, in about 3% of infected patients, most often in children aged 5-15.
  • Antibodies and CD4+ T cells against streptococcal M proteins cross-react with self antigens in the heart.
  • Aschoff bodies are pathognomonic: focal necrosis, T lymphocytes and Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells with a slender wavy ribbon of chromatin.
  • Pancarditis: fibrinous "bread and butter" pericarditis, myocarditis, and small vegetations along the lines of closure over fibrinoid necrosis (mitral 65%, aortic 25%).

Source: Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever)

Pathology · 9

Jones criteria

How it works

Because no single test proves rheumatic fever, the Jones criteria combine clinical features with evidence of a recent group A strep infection.

What to do first

  1. Count majors and minors, then check for strep evidence.
  2. Diagnose with 2 major, or 1 major + 2 minor, plus strep evidence.

Client example

Chorea + fever + raised ESR + high antibody titer = 1 major + 2 minor with evidence: criteria met.

Common trap

Calling arthralgia a major criterion; migratory polyarthritis is major, arthralgia is minor.

Memory trick

Majors spell J-O-N-E-S: Joints, O (carditis, the heart), Nodules, Erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • A prolonged on ECG is a minor criterion.
  • Subcutaneous nodules are firm, painless and found on surfaces.

Key ideas

  • Major: carditis, migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
  • Minor: fever, arthralgia, previous rheumatic fever, raised ESR, CRP or leukocytosis, prolonged PR interval.
  • Evidence of preceding group A strep: positive throat culture or rapid antigen test, or raised or rising streptococcal antibody titer.
  • Diagnosis: 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor, supported by evidence of preceding group A streptococcal infection.
  • Migratory polyarthritis of large joints is self-limited with no chronic deformities.

Source: Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever)

Pathology · 10

Chronic rheumatic heart disease and mitral stenosis

How it works

Each attack of rheumatic endocarditis heals by fibrosis; repeated infections reactivate it, scarring the valves over decades. A scarred mitral valve narrows (fish mouth), blood dams up behind it in the left atrium and lungs, and the right heart eventually fails.

What to do first

  1. In mitral stenosis, monitor for atrial fibrillation, thromboembolism and right heart failure.
  2. Remember surgery (repair or replacement) has greatly improved the outlook.

Client example

A 9-year-old from an endemic area with recurrent fever, lung crackles and an apical diastolic murmur dies of rheumatic heart disease.

Common trap

Expecting the left ventricle to enlarge in pure mitral stenosis; it is largely unaffected.

Memory trick

Fish mouth valve, flooded lungs, failing right heart.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The mitral valve in chronic RHD looks like a or buttonhole.

Key ideas

  • Endocarditis of ARF heals by fibrosis; repeated pharyngeal infections reactivate the disease and scar the valves.
  • Mitral valve most commonly affected, then aortic; fibrosis of the leaflets leads to stenosis ("fish mouth" or "buttonhole").
  • Usually becomes clinically manifest decades after ARF.
  • Mitral stenosis: left atrial dilatation (with thrombi), chronic pulmonary venous congestion, lung fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, chronic right-sided failure; the left ventricle is largely unaffected.
  • Other complications: arrhythmias (especially atrial fibrillation), thromboembolism, infective endocarditis.

Source: Pathology L3 slides (rheumatic fever)

Pathology · 11

Arteriosclerosis patterns

How it works

Arteriosclerosis is the umbrella term for stiff, thick arteries. Its three patterns differ in which vessel layer and size they hit: intima of large arteries (atherosclerosis), media of muscular arteries (Mönckeberg) or small arteries and arterioles (arteriolosclerosis).

What to do first

  1. Link arteriolosclerosis to hypertension and diabetes.
  2. Recognize onion-skinning as hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis.

Client example

A diabetic client's renal arterioles are thickened by amorphous protein: hyaline arteriolosclerosis.

Common trap

Putting Mönckeberg sclerosis in arterioles.

Memory trick

Athero = intima plaque; Mönckeberg = Media calcium; arteriolo = tiny vessels.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Mönckeberg medial sclerosis occurs in people older than .

Key ideas

  • Arteriosclerosis: thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls ("hardening of the arteries").
  • Atherosclerosis: the most frequent and important pattern.
  • Mönckeberg medial sclerosis: calcific deposits in muscular arteries in people older than 50.
  • Arteriolosclerosis: small arteries and arterioles, with hypertension and diabetes; hyaline (amorphous proteinaceous wall) and hyperplastic ("onion-skinning").

Source: Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis)

Pathology · 12

Atherosclerosis: risk factors, pathogenesis and plaque

How it works

In the response-to-injury view, atherosclerosis is chronic inflammation started by endothelial injury. Monocytes enter the intima, smooth muscle cells are recruited, both swallow lipid as foam cells, and smooth muscle proliferation and collagen turn the lesion into a fibrofatty plaque.

What to do first

  1. Target modifiable risk factors: hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, diabetes.
  2. Know the lesion sequence: fatty spot, fatty streak, atheroma.

Client example

A young client's aorta shows flat yellow foam-cell streaks that do not narrow the lumen: fatty streaks.

Common trap

Thinking fatty streaks obstruct flow.

Memory trick

Spot (under 1 mm), streak (1 cm, flat), plaque (raised, capped).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The earliest lesion of atherosclerosis is the .
  • The atheroma's lipid core is covered by a firm white .

Key ideas

  • Atherosclerosis: a chronic inflammatory disease of the arterial wall with intimal atheromas that protrude into the lumen and weaken the media.
  • Non-modifiable risk factors: increasing age, male gender, family history. Modifiable: hyperlipidemia (LDL), hypertension, cigarette smoking, diabetes mellitus.
  • Response to injury: chronic endothelial injury, endothelial dysfunction with monocyte adhesion, smooth muscle recruitment and macrophage activation, foam cells, then smooth muscle proliferation and collagen deposition.
  • Fatty spots (<1 mm, foam cells) are the earliest lesion; fatty streaks (1 cm or longer) are not significantly raised and do not disturb blood flow.
  • Atheroma: raised intimal patch with a soft yellow lipid core under a firm white fibrous cap; cells, ECM and lipid.

Source: Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis)

Pathology · 13

Complications and sites of atherosclerosis

How it works

A plaque causes disease by narrowing a lumen slowly or by changing suddenly: rupture, ulceration or erosion exposes material that triggers thrombosis, and hemorrhage into a plaque can expand or rupture it. Pressure atrophy of the media leads to aneurysm.

What to do first

  1. Suspect acute plaque change behind a sudden MI or stroke.
  2. Link each site to its disease: coronary IHD, cerebral stroke, aorta aneurysm, legs gangrene.

Client example

A client with known coronary plaques suddenly has an MI: plaque rupture with thrombosis.

Common trap

Blaming calcification for the acute event.

Memory trick

Rupture, bleed, shower, bulge, calcify: the five plaque complications.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Rupture and hemorrhage into a plaque are called .

Key ideas

  • Common sites: lower abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal and internal carotid arteries, and the circle of Willis.
  • Acute plaque changes: rupture, ulceration or erosion (induces thrombosis), and fissure with hemorrhage into the plaque.
  • Other complications: atheroembolism, aneurysm from weakened media, calcification.
  • Consequences: ischemic heart disease (coronary), stroke (cerebral), aortic aneurysm (aorta), peripheral vascular disease with gangrene (leg arteries).

Source: Pathology L4 slides (atherosclerosis)

Pharmacology

Pharmacology · 1

Hypertension: definition and drug classes

How it works

Blood pressure is cardiac output times peripheral resistance, kept up by volume, the sympathetic system and the renin-angiotensin system. Each drug class removes one of these supports: diuretics (volume), sympatholytics (nerves), RAS drugs (angiotensin), CCBs and vasodilators (vessel tone).

What to do first

  1. Classify every drug on a client's list before giving it.
  2. Use the current threshold: 130/80 mm Hg or higher is hypertension.

Client example

A client's readings average 132/82: hypertension by the ACC/AHA and SHA definitions.

Common trap

Using the old 140/90 threshold.

Memory trick

-pril = ACE inhibitor, -sartan = ARB, -olol = beta blocker, -dipine = dihydropyridine CCB.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The only renin inhibitor listed is .

Key ideas

  • Hypertension is defined as 130/80 mm Hg or higher (ACC/AHA 2023 and Saudi Heart Association).
  • Classes: diuretics, calcium channel blockers, drugs acting on the renin-angiotensin system, sympatholytic drugs, vasodilators.
  • Drug list: hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, furosemide, spironolactone (diuretics); clonidine, methyldopa, prazosin, propranolol, labetalol, esmolol (sympathoplegic); hydralazine, nitroprusside, minoxidil, diazoxide, fenoldopam, CCBs (vasodilators); captopril, enalapril, enalaprilat (ACE inhibitors); losartan (ARB); aliskiren (renin inhibitor).

Source: Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension)

Pharmacology · 2

Diuretics in hypertension

How it works

Diuretics lower pressure first by shrinking plasma volume and cardiac output. Over 4-8 weeks the volume recovers but resistance falls: sodium depletion lowers smooth muscle Na+, which lowers intracellular Ca++ through the Na/Ca exchanger, relaxing arterioles.

What to do first

  1. Use thiazides first in normal renal function; loop diuretics in CKD or malignant hypertension.
  2. Add a potassium-sparing diuretic to a thiazide to counteract hypokalemia; spironolactone for hyperaldosteronism.

Client example

A client 6 weeks into thiazide therapy has normal urine output but a lower blood pressure: peripheral resistance has fallen.

Common trap

Believing diuretics work only by making urine.

Memory trick

Thiazide first, Loop for kidney failure, K-sparing for K.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Diuretics can the hypotensive effects of many antihypertensive agents.

Key ideas

  • Early: diuretics lower plasma volume and cardiac output. After 4-8 weeks volume and output return toward normal while peripheral vascular resistance falls (arteriolar vasodilation).
  • Main mechanism of the vasodilation: depletion of body Na+, lowering smooth muscle Na+ and then intracellular Ca++ via the Na/Ca exchanger.
  • Thiazides are first choice; antihypertensive doses are lower than diuretic doses.
  • Loop diuretics are preferable in malignant hypertension and chronic kidney disease.
  • Potassium-sparing diuretics are used with thiazides to counteract hypokalemia; spironolactone is used in hyperaldosteronism.

Source: Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension)

Pharmacology · 3

Calcium channel blockers

How it works

CCBs block L-type Ca++ channels, so less calcium enters smooth muscle (and, for verapamil and diltiazem, heart muscle). Dihydropyridines act on vessels only, so heart rate may rise; verapamil and diltiazem also slow the heart.

What to do first

  1. Expect a possible rise in heart rate with nifedipine and a fall with verapamil or diltiazem.
  2. Use nicardipine for hypertensive emergencies; avoid short-acting nifedipine.

Client example

A client starting nifedipine has a slightly faster pulse.

Common trap

Expecting nifedipine to slow the heart like verapamil.

Memory trick

Dihydropyridine = Dilates only; Verapamil = Ventricle too.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • CCBs are first-choice drugs and are more effective in patients.
  • Nicardipine has vascular selectivity.

Key ideas

  • CCBs bind the L-type voltage-gated Ca++ channel from the inner side of the membrane.
  • Verapamil and diltiazem block Ca++ channels in heart and vessels; dihydropyridines (nifedipine, nicardipine) block vessels only.
  • Heart rate: increased with dihydropyridines; unchanged or decreased with verapamil and diltiazem. Postural hypotension is negligible.
  • First-choice drugs, more effective in African patients; nicardipine for hypertensive emergencies; short-acting nifedipine increases mortality.

Source: Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension)

Pharmacology · 4

Renin inhibitors, ACE inhibitors and ARBs

How it works

Renin turns angiotensinogen into angiotensin I, ACE turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II (and breaks down bradykinin), and angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors. Blocking any step lowers angiotensin II effects; the step blocked decides the side effects: ACE inhibitors raise bradykinin (cough, angioedema), ARBs do not.

What to do first

  1. Monitor potassium, renal function, first-dose blood pressure and the airway (angioedema).
  2. Question ACE inhibitors and ARBs in pregnancy and bilateral renal artery stenosis.
  3. Switch to an ARB when an ACE inhibitor causes cough.

Client example

A client on captopril develops a dry cough and is switched to losartan.

Common trap

Thinking losartan inhibits ACE.

Memory trick

ACE inhibitors Accumulate bradykinin; ARBs Avoid it.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The ACE inhibitor given intravenously is .
  • ARBs selectively block receptors.

Key ideas

  • Aliskiren competitively inhibits renin: angiotensin I, II and aldosterone fall and renin rises; hyperkalemia when combined with ACE inhibitors or ARBs.
  • ACE inhibitors block conversion of angiotensin I to II and raise bradykinin; less angiotensin II removes negative feedback, so renin rises.
  • Captopril, lisinopril and enalaprilat are active drugs; enalapril, benazepril and fosinopril are prodrugs activated by the liver; enalaprilat is the IV form.
  • ACE inhibitor adverse effects: first-dose hypotension, dry cough (bradykinin, prostaglandins or substance P), renal insufficiency in bilateral renal artery stenosis, hyperkalemia, angioedema; pregnancy category D.
  • ARBs (losartan) selectively block AT1 receptors, inhibit angiotensin more completely and have no effect on bradykinin; contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis and pregnancy.

Source: Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension)

Pharmacology · 5

Centrally acting sympatholytics

How it works

Clonidine and methyldopa act in the brain: they stimulate central alpha-2 (and, for clonidine, imidazoline) receptors that turn down sympathetic outflow. Methyldopa first has to be converted to methylnorepinephrine inside neurons.

What to do first

  1. Teach clients on clonidine never to stop it suddenly.
  2. Prefer methyldopa in pregnancy.
  3. Expect sedation; check for a positive Coombs' test with methyldopa.

Client example

A client on clonidine wants to stop abruptly; the nurse warns of a hypertensive crisis.

Common trap

Thinking methyldopa is unsafe in pregnancy.

Memory trick

Clonidine: don't Cut it suddenly. Methyldopa: Mothers.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Transdermal clonidine causes skin eruption in up to of clients.

Key ideas

  • Clonidine and methyldopa are alpha-2 receptor agonists; methyldopa is a false neurotransmitter converted to methylnorepinephrine; clonidine also acts on imidazoline receptors in the medulla.
  • The final common effect is a decrease in central adrenergic tone.
  • Second-choice drugs; methyldopa is often preferred in pregnancy.
  • Adverse effects: sedation, depression, bradycardia, AV block, sexual dysfunction; clonidine withdrawal can cause a hypertensive crisis; methyldopa can cause a positive Coombs' test.

Source: Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension)

Pharmacology · 6

Alpha blockers, beta blockers and alpha-beta blockers

How it works

Alpha-1 blockers dilate arterioles and veins, so standing can drop the pressure, especially after the first dose. Beta blockers lower cardiac output and renin release and leave veins alone, so they do not cause postural hypotension but can slow the heart, narrow airways and mask or cause low glucose.

What to do first

  1. After a first prazosin dose, monitor for postural hypotension.
  2. Choose a beta-1 selective drug (atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol) when airways are a concern.
  3. Never stop a beta blocker abruptly: rebound hypertension.

Client example

A client with heart failure and hypertension is treated with carvedilol.

Common trap

Expecting postural hypotension from a pure beta blocker.

Memory trick

A for alpha-1 and Arise-dizzy; B for beta and Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Blood sugar low.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • IV is used for hypertensive emergencies.
  • Peripheral edema with alpha blockers after chronic treatment is due to retention.

Key ideas

  • Prazosin and doxazosin selectively block alpha-1 receptors, dilating resistance and capacitance vessels; postural hypotension after the first dose ("first-dose phenomenon").
  • Beta blockers lower cardiac output (cardiac beta-1) and inhibit renin release (juxtaglomerular beta-1); they do not cause postural hypotension.
  • Selective beta-1: atenolol, bisoprolol, metoprolol. Non-selective: propranolol, penbutolol, timolol.
  • Beta-blocker adverse effects: bradycardia, rebound hypertension on abrupt withdrawal, bronchoconstriction, insomnia, depression, hypoglycemia, sexual dysfunction.
  • Labetalol and carvedilol block alpha and beta; labetalol for hypertension in pregnancy and IV in emergencies; carvedilol for heart failure.

Source: Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension)

Pharmacology · 7

Direct vasodilators

How it works

Direct vasodilators relax vessel smooth muscle by different routes: NO (nitroprusside), K+ channel opening (minoxidil, diazoxide), D1 activation (fenoldopam) or an uncertain mechanism (hydralazine). Their toxicities are drug-specific and well worth memorizing.

What to do first

  1. During nitroprusside infusion, watch for cyanide toxicity.
  2. Check glucose with diazoxide, hair growth with minoxidil, lupus-like symptoms with high-dose hydralazine.
  3. Question fenoldopam in glaucoma, angina or hypokalemia.

Client example

A client on minoxidil notices new hair growth: hypertrichosis.

Common trap

Expecting diazoxide to cause diuresis like a thiazide.

Memory trick

Nitroprusside: Nitric oxide and cyaNide. Minoxidil: More hair. Diazoxide: Diabetes-like sugar.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Nitroprusside is metabolized by red blood cells, releasing cyanide that becomes .
  • Hydralazine is combined with isosorbide mononitrate in .

Key ideas

  • Nitroprusside: arterioles and veins, nitric oxide; metabolized by red cells releasing cyanide (to thiocyanate); half-life about 2 minutes, continuous infusion; for emergencies, severe heart failure, controlled hypotension.
  • Hydralazine: arterioles, uncertain mechanism; headache, palpitations, flushing; immunological lupoid syndrome (up to 20% at very high doses).
  • Minoxidil: arteriolar K+ channel opener, a prodrug; salt and water retention, tachycardia, hypertrichosis; also used for baldness.
  • Diazoxide: K+ channel opener without diuresis (lacks a sulfonamide group); salt and water retention, hyperglycemia; for hypertensive emergencies.
  • Fenoldopam: IV D1 agonist, renal and mesenteric vasodilation and natriuresis; reflex tachycardia, raised intraocular pressure, low potassium; contraindicated in angina, glaucoma and hypokalemia.

Source: Pharmacology L2-L4 slides (treatment of hypertension)

Biochemistry

Biochemistry · 1

Blood lipids and coronary heart disease

How it works

Cholesterol travels in blood packed in lipoproteins. LDL carries it to tissues and raises coronary risk; HDL is associated with lower risk. Lowering LDL by diet or drugs lowers risk.

What to do first

  1. Encourage diet control and expect a 10-20% fall; expect 30-40% with statins.
  2. Read a high HDL as protective.

Client example

A client with high LDL asks whether diet alone is enough: it lowers LDL by about 10-20%.

Common trap

Treating all cholesterol as bad: high HDL lowers risk.

Memory trick

LDL = Lousy, HDL = Helpful.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Elevated cholesterol increases the risk of CHD.

Key ideas

  • Total blood cholesterol comes from diet and endogenous synthesis and is carried by lipoproteins, especially LDL and HDL.
  • CHD risk rises with total and LDL cholesterol; high HDL-cholesterol is associated with decreased risk.
  • Diet control lowers TC and LDL-C by 10-20%; statins lower them by 30-40%.

Source: Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD)

Biochemistry · 2

Types of dietary fat and their effects

How it works

A fat's effect depends on its fatty acids: saturation, the number and position of double bonds, and cis or trans shape. Omega numbers count from the methyl end to the first double bond.

What to do first

  1. Advise limiting saturated and trans fats.
  2. Suggest olive oil (MUFA) and fatty fish (omega-3).
  3. Teach the label clue "partially hydrogenated".

Client example

A client switches butter for olive oil: LDL falls and HDL rises.

Common trap

Thinking omega-3 mainly lowers LDL; its main effect is on triacylglycerol, arrhythmia, thrombosis and inflammation.

Memory trick

SMASH fish for omega-3: salmon, mackerel, anchovies, sardines, herring.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Trans fats should be under of energy (under 2.2 g per day on 2000 kcal).
  • EPA has carbons and 5 double bonds; DHA has 22 carbons and 6.

Key ideas

  • Saturated fats (no double bonds; dairy, meat, coconut and palm oils) raise TC and LDL-C and CHD risk.
  • Monounsaturated fats (one double bond; olive oil, oleic acid, omega-9) lower TC and LDL-C and raise HDL-C when substituted for saturated fats.
  • Omega-6 fats (first double bond at carbon 6 from the methyl end; corn, sesame, cottonseed, sunflower oils) lower TC and LDL-C but also lower HDL-C and are proinflammatory.
  • Omega-3 fats suppress arrhythmia, reduce blood triacylglycerol, decrease thrombosis and inflammation, with little effect on LDL-C and HDL-C.
  • Trans fats are chemically unsaturated but behave like saturated fats: they raise LDL-C and lower HDL-C; formed by partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils (margarine).

Source: Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD)

Biochemistry · 3

Dietary cholesterol, plant sterols and cholesterol-lowering factors

How it works

Dietary cholesterol matters less than the fat mix. Plant sterols compete with cholesterol in the gut, so less is absorbed and LDL falls.

What to do first

  1. Correct a client who focuses only on dietary cholesterol.
  2. Suggest plant-sterol margarines, fiber and MUFA.

Client example

A client says eaten cholesterol matters more than fat type: needs further teaching.

Common trap

Thinking plant foods contain cholesterol.

Memory trick

Cholesterol only comes with a face (animal products).

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Plant sterols reduce LDL by inhibiting intestinal of cholesterol.

Key ideas

  • Dietary cholesterol is found only in animal products; its effect on blood cholesterol is less important than the amount and type of fatty acids.
  • Plant sterols reduce LDL-cholesterol by inhibiting intestinal absorption of cholesterol.
  • Dietary factors that decrease blood cholesterol: omega-6 PUFA, MUFA, antioxidants (beta carotene, vitamins E and C), plant sterols, vegetable fiber, large-dose vitamin B3.

Source: Biochemistry L5 slides (diet fat and CHD)

Biochemistry · 4

Free radicals, ROS and RNS

How it works

A free radical has an unpaired outer electron and steals one from the nearest molecule, starting chain damage to lipids, proteins and DNA. Non-radicals have no unpaired electron but are strong oxidants. Damage occurs when oxidants outrun antioxidants.

What to do first

  1. Classify each species as radical or non-radical.
  2. Separate endogenous (metabolism, phagocytosis) from exogenous (drugs, radiation, smoke) sources.

Client example

A smoker has an exogenous source of free radicals in cigarette smoke.

Common trap

Calling H2O2 a radical.

Memory trick

Radicals end with a dot: O2.-, OH., NO.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • Peroxynitrite is a reactive nitrogen .

Key ideas

  • Oxidative stress: an imbalance favoring oxidants and/or disfavoring antioxidants, potentially leading to damage.
  • A free radical is a molecule with an unpaired electron in an outer valence shell; it plucks an electron from the nearest molecule.
  • ROS radicals: superoxide, hydroxyl, peroxyl. ROS non-radicals: hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous acid, ozone.
  • RNS radicals: nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide. RNS non-radical: peroxynitrite.
  • Endogenous sources: electron leak from the respiratory chain, oxidases (xanthine oxidase), prostaglandin synthesis, NO from arginine, phagocytosis. Exogenous: drug metabolism (halothane, cytochrome P450), ionizing radiation, cigarette smoke.

Source: Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress)

Biochemistry · 5

Respiratory burst, nitric oxide and antioxidants

How it works

Reactive species are also tools. Neutrophils make superoxide, H2O2 and hypochlorous acid to kill bacteria. Endothelial NO dilates vessels. Antioxidant enzymes and nutrients keep the balance.

What to do first

  1. Link sepsis and inflammation to large iNOS output.
  2. Explain nitroglycerin works by becoming NO.

Client example

A client's angina is relieved by nitroglycerin, which is metabolized to nitric oxide.

Common trap

Mixing up constitutive eNOS (low, steady) with inducible iNOS (large, prolonged).

Memory trick

i for inducible and inflammatory.

Test yourself tap each blank

  • The enzyme that converts H2O2 and chloride into hypochlorous acid is .
  • NO synthase uses as its precursor.

Key ideas

  • Respiratory burst: NADPH oxidase converts O2 to superoxide; superoxide dismutase makes H2O2; myeloperoxidase converts H2O2 and chloride to hypochlorous acid, which kills bacteria.
  • NO is a free radical gas with a half-life of seconds, made from L-arginine by NO synthase.
  • eNOS and nNOS are constitutive and make low levels of NO; iNOS (macrophages, neutrophils; induced by bacterial toxins, TNF, cytokines) makes large amounts for hours or days.
  • eNOS-derived NO improves vascular dilation and perfusion; nitroglycerin is metabolized to NO and relieves coronary spasm in angina.
  • Enzymatic antioxidants: superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase. Nutrient antioxidants: vitamins A, E, C, selenium. Metabolic: glutathione, ceruloplasmin, albumin, transferrin, ferritin, uric acid.

Source: Biochemistry L6 slides (oxidative stress)

Biochemistry · 6

Oxidized LDL and the stages of atherosclerosis

How it works

Oxidation turns LDL into a danger signal. Oxidized LDL in the intima activates endothelium to recruit monocytes; macrophages take it up by scavenger receptors and become foam cells. Smooth muscle cells build a cap, dead cells pile up into a necrotic core, and a vulnerable plaque can rupture.

What to do first
